editorial.question: Which transmitter EVM allowance gives a useful 1024-QAM uplink advantage after practical hardware and receiver constraints?
editorial.answer: A looser allowance helps only if recovered power compensates its link-performance penalty; the 7 GHz submissions need aligned hardware assumptions and success criteria.
editorial.mechanism: An EVM allowance changes the amplifier error budget and back-off, while distortion changes the SNR required for useful throughput. Oscillator error and receiver configuration affect that balance.
editorial.tradeoff: One error limit simplifies MPR sets and testing; frequency-dependent allowances can accommodate different amplifier/oscillator budgets. The published evaluation metrics also differ.
editorial.consequence: An evaluator needs matched receiver/impairment conditions and practical output power, not just a comparison of proposed percentages.
editorial.novelty: Identifies the metric mismatch and missing common hardware budget, and connects the proposals to LG receiver-dependency evidence.
editorial.uncertainty: Referenced simulation reports not independently reviewed; extracted Ericsson setup/result channel labels differ and evaluation-set membership is unresolved.
editorial.analysis_excerpt: If the stricter limit delivers a useful throughput advantage at the output power that a practical 7 GHz transmitter can sustain, the single-limit approach avoids an additional requirements split. If its amplifier and oscillator budget forces enough power reduction to erase that advantage, an allowance for 7 GHz hardware has a stronger case. The common comparison still needed is useful throughput at a practical transmit-power operating point, with matched receiver and impairment assumptions.

claims.claim: A transmitter can send a cleaner radio signal by reducing its output power. It can also send a stronger signal with more distortion. The 6G fixed-wireless uplink question is which choice leaves the base station with more useful throughput. Samsung and Ericsson's November submissions propose different error limits at 7 GHz, but their more important disagreement concerns how to judge that balance.

claims.claim: For this decision, the distortion budget includes more than the power amplifier. Samsung discusses amplifier distortion, transceiver nonlinearity, local-oscillator phase noise and in-phase/quadrature imbalance. Its argument is that reducing output power mainly improves the amplifier contribution; it does not remove the other errors at the same rate. A looser overall EVM limit therefore cannot be translated directly into an equally large improvement in received signal quality.

claims.passage: On the other hand, the back-off saved by relaxing the 4GHz Tx EVM from 2.5% to 2.8% is small. Assuming about 1% each for the transceiver non-linearity, LO phase noise and IQ imbalance at 4GHz, the PA contribution is about 1.8% for 2.5% Tx EVM and grows only to about 2.2% for 2.8% Tx EVM, i.e., by about 1.7dB. At the rate of about 1dB of back-off per 2dB of EVM, this saves only about 0.9dB of back-off. A 0.9dB higher output power can give at most a 0.9dB higher SNR at the BS, which is much smaller than the about 3dB increase of the crossover SNR. Therefore, relaxing the 4GHz Tx EVM from 2.5% to 2.8% reduces the net gain of UL 1024QAM rather than making UL 1024QAM easier to use.

claims.claim: Power back-off is the reduction in amplifier operating power used to meet the signal-quality constraint. The requirements discussion expresses this power cost through maximum power reduction (MPR). Samsung argues that choosing EVM during the study already constrains the amplifier linearity and the MPR that will be specified later. Deferring the final power requirement does not make the current distortion decision independent of power.

claims.passage: The remaining question is whether 2.5% can be supported with a practical MPR. In [5], the PC2 MPR was evaluated with 2.5% Tx EVM over the full RB allocation space. The resulting MPR is 8dB for CP-OFDM and 5dB for DFT-s-OFDM. This means that the PC2 MPR evaluated with 2.5% Tx EVM without DPD is only 0.5dB to 1.5dB larger than the existing NR 256QAM MPR. The exact MPR will be decided in the WI phase. However, this result shows that 2.5% does not need DPD and can be supported with an MPR close to the 256QAM level. Therefore, for the feasibility conclusion of the SI, 2.5% Tx EVM, which is proven in the LLS, can be agreed for 4GHz.

claims.claim: Samsung uses crossover signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) as its link-performance test: the point where uplink 1024-QAM starts to deliver more throughput than 256-QAM. A higher crossover means the link needs better conditions before the higher-order modulation earns its place. In the single-layer results Samsung discusses at 4 GHz, relaxing transmitter EVM from 2.5% to 2.8% raises that crossover by roughly 3 decibels.

claims.passage: For 4GHz, the averaged LLS results from companies in RAN4#119 are shown in Figure 1 [3]. Between 2.5%+2.5% and 2.8%+2.5% (Tx EVM + Rx EVM), only the Tx EVM is changed, so this pair directly shows the impact of the Tx EVM. For all Rank 1 cases, the crossover SNR increases by about 3dB (2.7dB to 3.7dB) when the Tx EVM is relaxed from 2.5% to 2.8%, e.g., from 23.7dB to 26.7dB for MCS23 in TDL-D. For Rank 2 in TDL-A, the crossover SNR increases from about 31dB to about 46dB, which is beyond the practical SNR range of FWA. A similar trend is shown in [4], where the crossover SNR for MCS24 increases by 1.5dB to 2.8dB from 2.5%+2.5% to 3%+2.3%. In other words, at 4GHz the crossover SNR is very sensitive to the Tx EVM, and the gain of UL 1024QAM is clearly achieved within a practical SNR range with 2.5% Tx EVM.

claims.claim: Samsung assumes a larger local-oscillator phase-noise contribution at 7 GHz: about 1.2%, compared with about 1% at 4 GHz. In its calculation, holding overall EVM at 2.5% leaves an amplifier contribution of about 1.7%, tighter than its roughly 1.8% allowance at 4 GHz. It estimates about one decibel of additional back-off compared with a 2.8% limit. Its proposed 2.8% consequently makes room for both oscillator and amplifier impairments.
claims.passage: At 7GHz, both the PA and LO contributions are larger than at 4GHz. PA gain and linearity generally degrade at higher frequency, so more PA distortion is expected at the same output power, and LO phase noise also increases with the carrier frequency. Assuming about 1.2% LO phase noise at 7GHz, compared with about 1% at 4GHz, and the same transceiver non-linearity and IQ imbalance as at 4GHz, a 2.5% Tx EVM at 7GHz would require the PA contribution to be reduced to about 1.7%. This is even tighter than about 1.8% at 4GHz despite the worse PA linearity, and costs about 1dB more back-off than 2.8% Tx EVM. With 2.8% Tx EVM, the PA contribution is about 2.1%, so the higher LO contribution is covered and some margin is also given to the PA. In other words, 2.8% for 7GHz covers the higher PA and LO contributions, while it keeps the MPR at about the same level as at 4GHz. A further relaxation to 3% saves only about 0.5dB of back-off, since the PA contribution grows only to about 2.36%, i.e., by about 1dB. Even if a larger LO contribution of about 1.5% is assumed at 7GHz, the back-off saved by the relaxation to 3% is only about 0.6dB. This is smaller than the about 1dB or more increase of the crossover SNR. Therefore, 2.8% is a reasonable Tx EVM for 7GHz.

claims.claim: Ericsson supplies a different part of the evidence. It reports a 7 GHz evaluation with 2.5% transmitter and receiver EVM, explicitly without phase noise. It says the higher modulation reaches 90% of its maximum throughput in the configurations identified in its text. That establishes a reported link-level result under the stated simulation assumptions. It does not, by itself, close Samsung's question about output power with a practical oscillator and amplifier budget.

claims.passage: For 7GHz, 2.5% was not included in the RAN4 LLS campaign [2], so there is no LLS basis to select it in the SI. claims.claim: Ericsson's case for 2.5% is also a requirements-design argument. It says a frequency-dependent limit would require separate MPR sets, corresponding conformance tests and a boundary between frequency categories. It points to the difficulty of applying a 4.2 GHz boundary to the 4400-4800 MHz range. One EVM value would permit one MPR set per device power class and waveform across bands.
claims.passage: In NR, the UE MPR is specified per power class and waveform and does not depend on the operating band. For higher-order modulation, the MPR is driven by the Tx EVM requirement. A frequency-dependent UE Tx EVM, e.g. following the BS DL 1024QAM split at 4.2 GHz in TS 38.104 [8], would require two sets of MPR for UL 1024QAM and the corresponding conformance tests. It would also require a frequency boundary: with 4.2 GHz, the 4400-4800 MHz range studied in TR 38.922 would fall in a different category than the 4 GHz evaluations. A single value avoids these issues and results in one MPR set per power class and waveform for all bands. Furthermore, four sources show that the MPR increase for 2.5% Tx EVM is limited to 0.5-1.5 dB, whether compared with the existing NR 256QAM MPR or with a more relaxed 1024QAM Tx EVM [3]-[6].

claims.claim: This creates a tradeoff between a uniform requirements structure and the allowance for frequency-dependent hardware impairments. Ericsson argues that the added power reduction for 2.5% is limited; Samsung estimates a different cost when it budgets the 7 GHz amplifier and oscillator contributions. The available text supports comparing those assumptions, rather than declaring either percentage intrinsically more efficient.

Its May RAN4#119 contribution reports that additional receive antennas lower crossover SNR in its evaluated configurations, while some four-layer cases never exceed 256-QAM throughput within the simulated range. claims.claim: Ericsson uses the receiver dependency to argue against a fixed layer restriction. It says the network selects transmission rank and modulation together, and can refrain from scheduling multiple layers when the channel or base-station configuration cannot support them. claims.claim: If the stricter limit delivers a useful throughput advantage at the output power that a practical 7 GHz transmitter can sustain, the single-limit approach avoids an additional requirements split. If its amplifier and oscillator budget forces enough power reduction to erase that advantage, an allowance for 7 GHz hardware has a stronger case. The common comparison still needed is useful throughput at a practical transmit-power operating point, with matched receiver and impairment assumptions.
claims.passage: In NR, the UE MPR is specified per power class and waveform and does not depend on the operating band. For higher-order modulation, the MPR is driven by the Tx EVM requirement. A frequency-dependent UE Tx EVM, e.g. following the BS DL 1024QAM split at 4.2 GHz in TS 38.104 [8], would require two sets of MPR for UL 1024QAM and the corresponding conformance tests. It would also require a frequency boundary: with 4.2 GHz, the 4400-4800 MHz range studied in TR 38.922 would fall in a different category than the 4 GHz evaluations. A single value avoids these issues and results in one MPR set per power class and waveform for all bands. Furthermore, four sources show that the MPR increase for 2.5% Tx EVM is limited to 0.5-1.5 dB, whether compared with the existing NR 256QAM MPR or with a more relaxed 1024QAM Tx EVM [3]-[6].

claims.claim: If the stricter limit delivers a useful throughput advantage at the output power that a practical 7 GHz transmitter can sustain, the single-limit approach avoids an additional requirements split. If its amplifier and oscillator budget forces enough power reduction to erase that advantage, an allowance for 7 GHz hardware has a stronger case. claims.passage: At 7GHz, both the PA and LO contributions are larger than at 4GHz. PA gain and linearity generally degrade at higher frequency, so more PA distortion is expected at the same output power, and LO phase noise also increases with the carrier frequency. Assuming about 1.2% LO phase noise at 7GHz, compared with about 1% at 4GHz, and the same transceiver non-linearity and IQ imbalance as at 4GHz, a 2.5% Tx EVM at 7GHz would require the PA contribution to be reduced to about 1.7%. This is even tighter than about 1.8% at 4GHz despite the worse PA linearity, and costs about 1dB more back-off than 2.8% Tx EVM. With 2.8% Tx EVM, the PA contribution is about 2.1%, so the higher LO contribution is covered and some margin is also given to the PA. In other words, 2.8% for 7GHz covers the higher PA and LO contributions, while it keeps the MPR at about the same level as at 4GHz. A further relaxation to 3% saves only about 0.5dB of back-off, since the PA contribution grows only to about 2.36%, i.e., by about 1dB. Even if a larger LO contribution of about 1.5% is assumed at 7GHz, the back-off saved by the relaxation to 3% is only about 0.6dB. This is smaller than the about 1dB or more increase of the crossover SNR. Therefore, 2.8% is a reasonable Tx EVM for 7GHz.

claims.claim: A follow-up evaluation should place the candidate EVM limits on the same throughput-versus-link-budget comparison, include the oscillator and amplifier errors consistently, and state both crossover and near-maximum-throughput criteria. The unresolved choice is how much practical output power each distortion allowance costs, and whether the resulting link retains the gain used to justify 1024-QAM.
claims.passage: In RAN4#120bis, it was agreed that IQ imbalance and carrier leakage are considered as part of the Tx EVM requirement, without dedicated requirements [2]. For the down-selection, two aspects need to be considered together. The first is the gain of UL 1024QAM shown in the RAN4 LLS, i.e., the SNR (or SINR) at which UL 1024QAM starts to outperform UL 256QAM (crossover SNR). The second is the output power cost of the Tx EVM. Although the MPR is postponed to the WI phase, the Tx EVM agreed in the SI sets the PA linearity needed and hence the MPR to be specified later. As shown in [5], only the PA part of the Tx EVM changes with output power, by about 2dB for each 1dB of back-off, while the other parts, e.g., LO phase noise, do not. In other words, a tighter PA contribution costs about 1dB of back-off per 2dB of EVM, and a relaxed PA contribution saves back-off at the same rate. Therefore, each Tx EVM candidate should be judged by comparing the change in the crossover SNR with the change in back-off.
